name: Topical rapamycin

lead: Longevity-minded users apply rapamycin (sirolimus) cream hoping to slow visible skin aging and keep a younger-looking complexion.

Rapamycin, first isolated in 1972 from Easter Island soil bacteria, binds FKBP12 and inhibits mTOR, a pathway linked to aging in animal research. Topical sirolimus gel is approved for facial angiofibromas in tuberous sclerosis (FDA 2022, EU 2023). For aging skin, one small exploratory randomized trial reported reduced markers of senescence in human skin.

paras: It is a prescription drug, so people get it through a prescriber or compounding route and apply it to the skin as a cream or gel. Use for aging skin is off-label.

Oral sirolimus carries serious systemic risks, including infections, raised lipids, lung toxicity and impaired wound healing. Topical use in trials mostly caused mild irritation. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Longevity-minded users apply rapamycin cream hoping to slow visible skin aging. It inhibits mTOR in skin, which is linked to cell aging, so signs of aging may slow. Topical forms are approved for a rare facial condition, and one small exploratory trial reported reduced senescence markers in skin.

lead: Rapamycin, also called sirolimus, is a macrolide compound first isolated in 1972 from soil bacteria on Easter Island (Rapa Nui), and it inhibits the protein mTOR. It is approved as an oral immunosuppressant for transplant patients and for the lung disease lymphangioleiomyomatosis. Topical formulations are approved for facial angiofibromas, the small red facial bumps of tuberous sclerosis complex, where the FDA approved a sirolimus gel in 2022 and the EU authorised Hyftor in 2023 [1][2].

For appearance, topical rapamycin matters in two ways. In angiofibromas, trials show visibly smoother, less red facial skin, which is a documented cosmetic and medical outcome [3][2]. In anti-aging circles, it is discussed as a skin-aging intervention based on mTOR's role in aging; a small exploratory randomised trial in people over 40 with photoaging reported lower senescence markers and improved clinical and histological features of skin [4].

Systematic reviews describe topical sirolimus as increasingly used off-licence for other skin conditions, with the strongest randomised evidence in facial angiofibromas and mixed evidence in port-wine stains [5]. The drug is prescription-only in the US and EU, and cosmetic anti-aging use is research and off-label rather than labelled [1].

paras: In anti-aging circles, people discuss applying sirolimus-containing creams to the face to slow skin aging, reasoning that mTOR drives aging and that lowering mTOR activity in skin will reduce senescent cells. Wikipedia discusses topical rapamycin for skin aging only as research [1]. The one randomised study of this use enrolled people over 40 with photoaging and dermal volume loss [4].

The appearance goal people describe is firmer, less photodamaged-looking skin, while in tuberous sclerosis the goal is flatter, less red facial bumps. Angiofibromas appear in roughly three-quarters of people with the condition, usually start in childhood and can be socially distressing; laser treatment is painful and can leave scarring or pigment change, which is part of why a topical option drew interest [6][3].

Topical rapamycin is approved and used for facial angiofibromas in tuberous sclerosis. A 2010 report and small pilot studies suggested benefit [7][8], and a double-blind randomised trial evaluated safety and efficacy in these lesions [9]. The multicentre TREATMENT trial reported marked improvement (see Clinical studies) [3]. A review summarised in Wikipedia of 16 studies in 84 patients reported improvement in roughly 94%, with mostly mild skin irritation [1]. A French review notes that trials show significant but transient efficacy on angiofibroma size and visibility, with better results in younger patients than adults [10].

It has also been tested alongside pulsed dye laser for port-wine stains in Sturge-Weber syndrome [11], with earlier laboratory work on combined laser and topical rapamycin [12]. A 2024 systematic review included 71 studies and reported mixed evidence for port-wine stains, with effectiveness for sirolimus combined with pulsed-dye laser, and case reports of improvement in cutaneous vascular abnormalities [5]. A 2026 review of off-label uses lists pachyonychia congenita, trichilemmomas and trichoepitheliomas among the conditions with reported efficacy, noting small studies and variable formulations [13].

Sirolimus binds FKBP12, and the complex inhibits mTOR (mainly mTORC1), dampening cytokine signalling and slowing T and B cell activation. It does not act on calcineurin, unlike tacrolimus and ciclosporin [1]. mTOR is a kinase that integrates signals from insulin, growth factors, amino acids and energy status and regulates protein synthesis and autophagy. It was identified as the target of the rapamycin-FKBP12 complex in 1994, and mTOR activity helps drive the senescence-associated secretory phenotype [14]. In tuberous sclerosis, mutations in the hamartin-tuberin complex release mTOR from its normal brake, which promotes tumour formation, the basis for treating angiofibromas with an mTOR inhibitor [6].

A 2003 worm study linked mTORC1 to aging. Sirolimus has since extended lifespan in yeast, worms, flies and mice; a 2009 NIH study showed lifespan extension in wild-type mice, and a 2020 study found sex-specific effects with late-life dosing extending lifespan in males but not females. Two human studies found no statistically significant longevity benefit, though Wikipedia notes their limitations [1]. A 2014 Science Translational Medicine study of the related compound everolimus (RAD001) in elderly volunteers reported about a 20 percent better influenza vaccine response and fewer PD-1-positive T cells, which the authors described as a small study and not proof of clinical benefit [15]. Wikipedia's mTOR entry notes that rapamycin extends lifespan in mice across sexes, even when started late in life [14].
Animal work on skin includes studies in mice on skin tumour promotion [16] and psoriasis-like inflammation [17], which concern disease models rather than cosmetic aging.

Systemic sirolimus carries risks including peripheral oedema, raised cholesterol and triglycerides, low platelets, infections, impaired wound healing, lung toxicity (interstitial pneumonitis) and diabetes-like effects through mTORC2 inhibition. It may raise skin cancer and lymphoma risk [1]. Topical use in trials was generally associated with mild local effects. In the TREATMENT trial there was no measurable systemic absorption, drug-related events were at 10% or less incidence (application site discomfort, itch, redness, irritation), and nearly all were mild [3]. The EU product information lists application-site irritation, dry skin, acne and itching as the most common side effects of Hyftor, seen in more than 1 in 10 people [2]. A systematic review found ointments and once-daily use appeared to cause fewer side effects [5].

Sirolimus was isolated in 1972 from Streptomyces hygroscopicus in soil samples from Easter Island and named after the island's native name, Rapa Nui. It was first developed as an antifungal before its immunosuppressive and antiproliferative effects were discovered; a 1975 paper by Vezina, Kudelski and Sehgal described the producing organism and compound [1]. The FDA approved Rapamune oral solution in 1999 and tablets in August 2000 [1]. The mTOR protein itself was identified through yeast genetics in 1991 and as the drug's mammalian target in 1994 [14].

Topical use for angiofibromas began with a 2010 report in Archives of Dermatology [7]. Hyftor gel received a positive CHMP opinion on 23 February 2023 and an EU marketing authorisation on 15 May 2023 [2], and a sirolimus gel was approved in the US in 2022 [1].

Sirolimus is prescription-only in the US and EU [1]. Hyftor is authorised for adults and children aged 6 and older with tuberous sclerosis angiofibroma, has orphan medicine status, and treatment is stopped if there is no effect after 12 weeks [2].

Rapamycin and metformin are described as caloric restriction mimetics, and Wikipedia's life-extension entry notes researchers are exploring intermittent dosing to reduce side effects, while stating the FDA said in 2023 that no medication has been proven to slow or reverse aging [18]. Interest has continued: a 2026 Hacker News post links a trial of exercise combined with weekly sirolimus in older adults [19]. Topical skin use sits within this wider enthusiasm as a way to target skin directly with less systemic exposure, as trial authors have framed it [4].

Aging skin: a 2019 exploratory, prospective, placebo-controlled randomised trial (NCT03103893) in GeroScience by Chung and colleagues enrolled 36 people over 40 with photoaging and dermal volume loss. p16 INK4A, a senescence marker, fell significantly (P=0.008) and collagen VII rose (P=0.0077). Clinical skin appearance and histology improved in multiple participants. Of 36 enrolled, 19 discontinued or were lost to follow-up, leaving about 17 analysed, and the authors described the study as exploratory and a basis for further work [4].

TREATMENT trial: a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled trial at 9 US sites and 1 Australian site enrolled 179 patients with tuberous sclerosis facial angiofibromas (mean age 20.5 years). Participants applied 1% rapamycin, 0.1% rapamycin or vehicle nightly for six months. Mean improvement on the Angiofibroma Grading Scale was 16.7 points (1%), 11.0 (0.1%) and 2.1 (vehicle). Photographs were rated better than baseline in 81.8%, 65.5% and 25.5% respectively [3]. Most improvement occurred in the first month [3].

EU registration study: facial angiofibroma size and redness improved or greatly improved after 12 weeks in 18 of 30 patients (60%) using Hyftor, compared with none of 32 patients on placebo gel [2]. Other randomised trials include a rapamycin-calcitriol combination [20] and a novel cream formulation [21].

Reviews: a 2024 systematic review (71 studies) reported efficacy in angiofibromas across 799 patients compared with placebo, predominantly at 0.1% [5]. Cochrane reviews of rapamycin and rapalogs in tuberous sclerosis cover the wider condition [22].

Other facial studies: pilot studies reported benefit in small groups [7][8]; a phase II trial combined it with pulsed dye laser in Sturge-Weber port-wine stains [11], and a randomised trial compared pulsed dye laser, erbium YAG laser and topical sirolimus in port-wine stains [23]. These conditions are medical rather than cosmetic aging.

lore.intro: Topical rapamycin is discussed in longevity and anti-aging circles as a way to apply mTOR inhibition directly to facial skin, usually with reference to the 2019 GeroScience trial [4][19].
